title: Met Costume Institute to Honor John Galliano With Retrospective Despite Antisemitic Past
excerpt: The 2027 exhibition 'John Galliano: Horizons' marks only the third time the Met has dedicated a show to a living designer, reigniting debate over art and accountability.
body:
• The Metropolitan Museum of Art announced 'John Galliano: Horizons' as its 2027 Costume Institute exhibition, with the accompanying Met Gala expected on the first Monday of May.
  • It will be only the third time the Met has dedicated an exhibition to a living designer, following Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo in 2017.
  • Galliano was fired from Dior in 2011 after an antisemitic rant in which he declared 'I love Hitler,' and was convicted by a French court.
  • The Anti-Defamation League has said Galliano has genuinely worked to address his behavior, while Anna Wintour continues to support his rehabilitation.

Fashion's Most Controversial Honor

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute will dedicate its marquee 2027 exhibition to John Galliano, the brilliantly talented and deeply controversial British designer whose career was derailed by antisemitic outbursts in 2011. The show, titled John Galliano: Horizons, was announced on Friday.

The retrospective will open in May 2027, with the year's Met Gala — fashion's most prominent annual event — also expected to center on Galliano's work. It represents a definitive institutional endorsement of the designer's rehabilitation, one that will test how the fashion world navigates the tension between artistic achievement and personal accountability.

A Rare and Loaded Distinction

Only two living designers have previously received a solo Costume Institute exhibition: Yves Saint Laurent in 1983, organized by Diana Vreeland, and Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons in 2017. The honor places Galliano in rarefied company and signals the Met's confidence that the cultural conversation has shifted enough to absorb the inevitable backlash.

"The moment can be particularly difficult now, given the alarming rise of hate. But that makes the question more urgent, not less."

— Andrew Bolton, Curator, Costume Institute

Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute's curator, told The New York Times that he had considered a Galliano retrospective since 2010 and had been seriously planning it for two years. He framed the exhibition as confronting, rather than evading, the designer's history.

The Fall and Rehabilitation

Galliano's career trajectory is one of fashion's most dramatic arcs. As creative director of Dior from 1996 to 2011, he was widely regarded as one of the most inventive designers of his generation, known for theatrical runway shows and technically audacious garments.

His downfall was swift. In 2011, a video surfaced of Galliano at a Paris bar declaring his love for Hitler and telling two women that their forebears would have been gassed. A French court convicted him of public insults based on religious affiliation, and Dior fired him immediately.

After years in treatment and relative obscurity, Galliano returned to fashion at Maison Margiela, where he spent a decade building critical acclaim and driving double-digit sales growth. He stepped down in December 2024 and in March 2026 signed a two-year creative partnership with Zara, with his first collection due in September.

Divided Reactions

The Anti-Defamation League's leader has said the organization believes Galliano has genuinely worked to address the issues behind his antisemitic outburst, and that his efforts at making amends should be recognized. Anna Wintour, who is no longer Vogue's editor but remains closely tied to the Met Gala, has never wavered in her support for the designer.

For the fashion industry's growing South Asian presence — from designers like Sabyasachi Mukherjee and Rahul Mishra to the increasing visibility of Indian craftsmanship on global runways — the Galliano exhibition poses a complex question: how an industry that struggles to make space for diverse voices can lavish its highest honor on a figure whose past actions targeted a marginalized community.
nri_angle: The choice raises uncomfortable questions for South Asian designers who have long sought greater representation at fashion's highest levels, while the exhibit tests how the industry reconciles artistic genius with personal conduct.
